新华社北京11月21日电　由新华通讯社发起的亚太媒体合作伙伴计划近日宣布正式成立，首批伙伴计划成员机构共计310家，覆盖亚太41个国家和地区。

在9月5日举行的亚太媒体高端论坛开幕式上，来自40多个国家和地区以及联合国机构、国际组织的400余名中外嘉宾共同见证了伙伴计划筹备委员会成立。筹委会发出《关于加强亚太媒体智库合作传播的倡议》，正式邀请亚太地区媒体、智库等机构加入伙伴计划。截至发稿日，共有310家机构加入，成为伙伴计划成员。

伙伴计划以加强亚太区域媒体互利共赢为目标，重点打造高端对话、协同传播、技术创新、务实合作四大平台，将机制化举办媒体高端对话活动，推动亚太地区媒体开展联合采访，合作制作优秀融媒产品，开展亚太地区媒体记者来华采访活动，举办亚太媒体主题研修活动等一系列务实合作项目。

《亚太媒体合作伙伴计划》及《亚太媒体高端论坛深圳共识》已纳入中国担任2026年亚太经合组织东道主成果清单。亚太媒体高端论坛已纳入中国担任2026年亚太经合组织东道主主办会议和活动清单。

items.title: JEDEC Previews DDR6 Memory Standard: 2.35x More Bandwidth, 44% Narrower DIMMs
items.content:
It is hard to believe that it has already been over 6 years since DDR5 memory was launched, but now in the fall of 2026 it is already time to start talking about the next generation of server memory.

This past week the JEDEC Solid State Technology Association, the industry consortium responsible for developing the various memory standards (among other specifications) released a preview of the in-development DDR6 memory standard.

The next generation of the group’s mainline SDRAM memory standard, DDR6’s development has been known about for quite some time now. But, outside of the customary bandwidth improvements, it has not been clear what other changes the DDR6 specification may bring with it. Now, following JEDEC’s preview, we have our first official look at what some of the major features of the new specification will be – or at least, are expected to be based on the current development plans.

## DDR6 Memory Standard Preview: Smaller DIMMs, Bigger Bandwidth

As always, the key improvement in a new generation of DDR memory is the amount of bandwidth available per DIMM. DDR6, in turn, is planned to be a major overhaul of DDR memory technology in this regard, as it is tackling the matter from both ends.

In regards to per-pin bitrates, the current plan calls for DDR6 to start at 12.8 GT/sec and eventually reach 14.4 GT/sec and higher. Currently, DDR5 tops out at 9.2 GT/sec, so at the top end this would represent an eventual 57% increase in per-pin bandwidth. Meanwhile looking at things on a contextual basis, the original DDR5 specification stopped at 6.4 GT/sec, so if DDR6 were to eventually end up on a similar long-term trajectory, then “beyond” could eventually extend well past 14.4 GT/sec.

Still, a 57% increase is not as much bandwidth as some customers would like to see, so the group is also planning to take the more radical step of changing the bit-width of a DIMM itself. Following nearly three decades of DIMMs being 64-bits wide, going back to the days of single data rate SDRAM, the group is proposing to make DIMMs even wider, moving to a 96-bit wide memory bus.

With 32 more data pins (DQ lines), a DDR6 DIMM would offer 50% more bandwidth at identical clockspeeds to a DDR5 DIMM. Or, combining the two improvements, a full DDR6-14400 DIMM would offer 172.8GB/sec of bandwidth, or 2.35x as much bandwidth as a DDR5-9200 DIMM does today (and more still compared to the DDR5-8000 DIMMs that the latest server platforms actually support).

The switch to a wider bus width for an individual DIMM will come with some significant ramifications for the rest of the standard as well, in part because of the changes that need to happen in order to enable those wider DIMMs. Key to this, DDR6 will be employing a pseudo-channel architecture that splits up the individual channels.

Unfortunately, JEDEC’s preview announcement does not clarify if and how this might interact with the sub-channel architecture that DDR5 currently employs, so we do not have enough information to definitively state how this compares to DDR5’s architecture in this regard. But broadly speaking, splitting up DIMMs into multiple channels is how the most recent version of the standard was able to raise bandwidth in light of DRAM core clockspeeds having long grown stagnant, and some kind of similar change has been expected for DDR6 as well.

Regardless, the specification is also doubling the number of memory banks on a DIMM, which by our reckoning should bring it up to 16 banks per group. This is another change that should further help DDR6 deliver data at those higher pin bitrates, as it affords more banks that can be used while the other banks are busy refreshing.

The change to the individual DIMM memory bus width will also bring with it some physical changes to DIMM designs – and more than you might be expecting. JEDEC will be introducing a more compact 74mm wide DIMM for DDR6, which on a relative basis is just a bit wider than a DDR5 SO-DIMM. According to the group, the change is being made to allow for systems with higher memory densities as, while routing small traces is bad enough, 16 channels of DDR5 DIMMs takes up an immense amount of physical space that there is no real work-around for with their 133mm module width.

Notably, the group’s announcement does not clarify whether they will keep the current DIMM width, which like the 64-bit memory bus has been with the standard since the earliest days. Though JEDEC is quick to note that they are working on multiple form factors, potentially including RDIMMs, UDIMMs, and even CAMMs – the latter of which was added to DDR5 as a mid-generation feature. In that respect, the denser 73mm form factor may end up as a premium option for RDIMMs, especially as a smaller connector combined with a wider memory bus would require some very small pins on the new compact form factor.

Meanwhile, it is interesting to see that, at present, there is no mention of SO-DIMMs at all. So the small laptop DIMM factor may very well be on its way out in favor of CAMMs (or soldiered memory) for all laptops.

On the other hand, the preview announcement mentions server needs front and center. JEDEC’s members are well-aware of the need for more memory in the data center, and this is something that the group is explicitly looking to tackle. In practice, this would seem to be aiming to deliver on all three major features that data center operators are after: smaller DIMMs, more memory bandwidth per DIMM, and higher capacities overall.

Speaking of which, besides allowing for more DIMMs in a given amount of space, the DDR6 specification will also be tackling the memory capacity matter from the other direction as well. As always, the latest standard is increasing the maximum supported die density, bringing it from 64 Gbit to 128 Gbit. At the same time, the spec will make some unspecified optimizations for die stacking to allow for higher capacity packages overall. At present, die stacked DRAM packages are far from brand new, but 3DS DIMMs are still relatively uncommon overall.

A bit more nebulous, the announcement also notes support for multiple ECC implementations. The current DDR5 standard has a single ECC standard at the DIMM level for transmission and overall DIMM reliability, as well as on-die ECC to protect/correct the individual cells. In the past year we have seen some proposals for layering additional soft ECC on top of this to further improve reliability (e.g. Astera Labs’ Leo CXL memory expanders), so it may be that JEDEC is eyeing something similar, to let customers allocate additional DRAM capacity to storing ECC data for even higher levels of reliability.

Finally, the DDR6 standard will be taking steps to rein in the power consumption of DIMMs, which has been a concern with every generation as increased performance comes will otherwise drive up the power needs. For the next version of the spec, DDR6 will be switching to VSS-terminated I/O, as opposed to DDR5’s VDDQ-based termination – in effect terminating with a low voltage instead of a high voltage. The spec will also introduce low power modes for data center use, though the initial announcement does not go into further detail. Regardless, the consortium is targeting “significantly improved performance-per-watt” versus DDR5, which would be welcome across the board, but especially in data centers where power is a constraining factor and large DIMM counts are eating up larger amounts of that budget.

## Final Words

Wrapping things up, JEDEC’s initial announcement for DDR6 emphasizes how the group has significant plans for the next generation of the memory standard. While it is true that every generation of DDR has been faster and lower power than the previous, how this is accomplished has changed with every generation – and it gets harder all the time. Meanwhile the physical DIMM changes are even more remarkable, and they underscore how the group is ready to break away from the form factors that have defined SDRAM for almost the last 30 years.

The net impact of these changes, in turn, stands to be significant. A 2.35x bandwidth increase on its own is quite remarkable. Accomplishing that while also shrinking the width of a DIMM by 44% is even more so. Consequently, DDR6 as currently proposed stands to be a big change indeed.

As for when we might see a complete specification, or better still physical DIMMs, that will have to wait. This preview was just that: an early look at a specification still under development, and a not-too-subtle reminder to the industry that if they want to see more and participate in the development process, they need to be part of the JEDEC. On which note, the JC-42 workgroup will be meeting in Hawaii at the end of this month for their final quarterly meeting of the year.

items.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
items.content:
# In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest

Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week

- Published

**An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.**

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.content:
# Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide

Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

- Published

**Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.**

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

items.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
items.content:
# French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler

The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio

- Published

**Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.**

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

  - Published27 November 2020

items.title: John Forsyth, Cirrus Logic President and CEO, Elected Chair of Semiconductor Industry Association
items.content:
The Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) today announced that Cirrus Logic (NASDAQ: [CRUS](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/john-forsyth-cirrus-logic-president-and-ceo-elected-chair-of-semiconductor-industry-association-302946167.html#financial-modal)) President and CEO John Forsyth has been elected Chair of the SIA [Board of Directors](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4827688-1&h=3197114258&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.semiconductors.org%2Fabout%2Fboard-of-directors%2F&a=Board+of+Directors). Tom Caulfield, Executive Chairman of GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ: [GFS](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/john-forsyth-cirrus-logic-president-and-ceo-elected-chair-of-semiconductor-industry-association-302946167.html#financial-modal)), was elected Vice Chair. AMD (NASDAQ: [AMD](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/john-forsyth-cirrus-logic-president-and-ceo-elected-chair-of-semiconductor-industry-association-302946167.html#financial-modal)) Chair and CEO Lisa Su, who served as 2026 Chair, will continue to serve on the Board and the Leadership Committee. SIA, the voice of the semiconductor industry, represents 99% of the U.S. semiconductor industry by revenue and nearly two-thirds of non-U.S. chip firms.

“Congratulations to John Forsyth on his election as SIA Chair. John has been a trusted partner since my first day at SIA, and he brings steady, strategic judgment to a pivotal year for our industry,” said SIA President and CEO Michael Robbins. “With a new Congress, SIA’s 50th anniversary, and the work of extending the Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit ahead of us, I look forward to working with John, Tom Caulfield, and our entire Board to strengthen America’s semiconductor leadership. I also want to thank Lisa Su for an outstanding year as our Chair. Her steadfast leadership strengthens SIA and our industry, and I am tremendously grateful for her guidance and counsel.”

Forsyth brings more than 20 years of experience in semiconductor industry leadership. As president and CEO of Cirrus Logic, he leads the company in developing high-precision, low-power audio and mixed-signal semiconductor solutions for a broad range of consumer, automotive, and industrial applications. Forsyth has served as president and chief executive officer of Cirrus Logic since January 2021. He joined the company in 2014 through its acquisition of Wolfson Microelectronics and was named president in 2020 after previous roles including chief strategy officer and vice president of marketing.

“I’m honored to serve as SIA Chair at such an important time for our industry,” said John Forsyth, president and CEO of Cirrus Logic. “America’s leadership in the next wave of semiconductor innovation depends on both a thriving domestic industry and close collaboration between that industry and government. I look forward to working with SIA’s Board of Directors and members to strengthen that collaboration, accelerate the build-out of a more resilient domestic supply chain, and keep the U.S. at the forefront of this critical technology.”

The post [John Forsyth, Cirrus Logic President and CEO, Elected Chair of Semiconductor Industry Association](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/john-forsyth-cirrus-logic-president-and-ceo-elected-chair-of-semiconductor-industry-association/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Digest](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com).

items.title: World’s First Mass Production of Ultrahigh-Mobility Oxide Technology Paves the Way for a New Generation of Displays
items.content:
TCL CSOT became the world’s first to achieve mass production of ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology (**electron** **mobility of ~50 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹**) on an 8.6-generation line. The major technical breakthrough marks the first time high mobility oxide technology has gone beyond the 50 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ threshold in mass production, presenting exciting new possibilities in display applications.

**Beyond 50 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹: Premium Displays Without the Compromise**

For years, the production of high-end displays has involved a series of trade-offs: high refresh rates versus lower power consumption, high resolution versus brightness, and narrow bezels versus cost. The mass production of ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology breaks this deadlock by enabling drive currents that surpass the critical threshold needed to deliver these properties without such compromises.

**All-Round Excellence in Image Quality, Energy Efficiency, and Cost**

Traditionally, gains in image quality have come at the expense of power consumption. However, the properties of ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology change this on several fronts. Firstly, like all oxide TFTs, the technology offers extremely low off-state current, enabling static images to be held at an ultra-low refresh rate, thereby reducing refresh power consumption. Secondly, higher current drive allows GOA (gate driver on array) and driver circuits to operate with lower voltage swings and shorter charging times. Combined with optimization across the full signal chain, power consumption is also reduced when displaying dynamic images. As a result, ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology allows for improvements in image quality without requiring extra power.

By enabling displays to switch between ultra-low and ultra-high refresh rates in the same panel, the technology also allows high-performance gaming and video applications to exist alongside power-efficient office and reading in one device.

Shrinking the TFT also increases aperture ratio, enabling higher pixel density without sacrificing brightness, so high-resolution screens no longer appear dim. Substantially reduced edge routing greatly improves the screen-to-body ratio, making ultra-narrow bezels a reality for mass-produced displays.

The real value of ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology is in turning what was once a series of trade-offs into a best-of-all-worlds scenario that delivers premium display experiences. Leveraging the scale of TCL CSOT’s 8.6-generation production line, these premium displays can now be widely adopted at an affordable cost.

At DTC 2026, TCL CSOT unveiled its own ultrahigh-mobility display technology, setting a new standard for display excellence that will redefine the future for both consumer and professional display applications.

**Technology Reimagined: A Seamless Loop from Process to Product**

Developing ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology is the result of significant engineering achievements made by TCL CSOT and the team at the Institute of Science Tokyo’s MDX Research Center for Element Strategy, led by Prof. Hideo Hosono. Together with Prof. Hosono’s team, TCL CSOT has advanced the technology across three fronts—film deposition, device design, and architecture—transforming isolated processes into manufacturable products.

**Film Deposition: Ultra-Uniform Oxide Semiconductor System**

TCL CSOT has taken film deposition beyond conventional processes with the use of continuous rotary-target sputtering and a composite stacked oxide layer design that suppresses defects. A defect repair process further improves the interface, overcoming the stability challenges associated with ultrahigh-mobility materials.

**Device Core: Precise Control of the Hydrogen–Oxygen Balance in the Insulator**

Ultrahigh-mobility devices are highly sensitive to moisture, hydrogen, and oxygen, and any deviation from the optimal hydrogen–oxygen ratio in the insulator can degrade performance. To address this, TCL CSOT has developed a hydrogen–oxygen balance control system for both the front- and back-channel insulators, providing threefold protection.

**New Circuit Architecture Unlocks the Potential of Ultrahigh-Mobility Oxide**

Alongside its clear benefits, higher mobility also brings new challenges, including weaker gate control, threshold-voltage drift, and increased self-heating. To address these challenges, TCL CSOT has introduced a new GOA architecture alongside optimized device design and improved thermal management to enable the full potential of ultrahigh-mobility oxide to be realized.

**Redefining the Limits of LCD Technology**

The mass production of ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology gives LCD a major competitive edge in applications such as high-refresh-rate notebooks and high-end monitors, enabling it to compete directly with OLED. Its inherent advantages—low cost, long lifetimes, and no burn-in—combined with high image quality and low power consumption, will offer users a wider choice of high-quality options at a lower price point compared with OLED.

Meanwhile, ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology also shows strong potential in emerging areas such as VR/AR, medical displays, and automotive displays, where its high refresh rates can help reduce motion sickness, its high color fidelity meets high professional requirements, and its high reliability supports use in diverse environments.

**From the Laboratory to the Production Line**

TCL CSOT has built extensive expertise in oxide technology over the years, progressing from mass production of conventional IGZO in 2024 to 30 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ high-mobility oxide in 2025, and achieving mass production of ultrahigh-mobility oxide in 2026. The latest breakthrough combines device stability comparable to conventional IGZO with excellent voltage endurance and reliability, marking a major step from the laboratory to production and lays the foundations for future product iterations and scale expansion.

The post [World’s First Mass Production of Ultrahigh-Mobility Oxide Technology Paves the Way for a New Generation of Displays](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/worlds-first-mass-production-of-ultrahigh-mobility-oxide-technology-paves-the-way-for-a-new-generation-of-displays/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Digest](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com).

items.title: Foundry-Compatible SiGe Trap-Rich Layer Technology Advances Next-Generation RF-SOI and FDSOI Platforms Share
items.content:
[Acorn Technologies](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Facorntech.com%2F&esheet=54644060&newsitemid=20261119466750&lan=en-US&anchor=Acorn+Technologies&index=1&md5=30a35164e5ba43176d4f34e51097ecdf), Inc., a semiconductor technology innovator focused on advanced process and device IP, today announced the results of its research collaboration with Jean-Pierre Raskin, PhD, full professor at the Université catholique de Louvain (UCLouvain), showing that Acorn Buried Stressor (ABS) technology can provide benefits for RF-SOI and FDSOI platforms: improved RF substrate performance through a next-generation silicon-germanium trap-rich layer (TRL) approach, with the additional benefit in FDSOI of faster transistor performance through silicon strain.

As foundries and system designers look beyond geometric scaling to improve performance, power efficiency and RF integration, FDSOI and RF-SOI platforms remain strategically important for low-power logic, wireless, mmWave, 5G Advanced and future 6G applications. ABS was originally developed as a proprietary buried stressor technology to make FDSOI logic devices faster and support FDSOI scaling. The UCLouvain collaboration revealed that Acorn’s buried silicon-germanium layer can also provide an RF benefit by functioning as a next-generation TRL, the RF-SOI substrate innovation Professor Raskin originally pioneered.

“These results show that ABS is far more than a logic-performance technology,” said Tom Horgan, CEO of Acorn. “ABS provides a potential path to extend FDSOI scaling by offering strain engineering in transistors while introducing a FDSOI-compatible trap-rich layer for improved RF-FDSOI circuit performance. ABS also offers the potential for a lower-cost, high-performance RF-SOI substrate that avoids the significant costs associated with a conventional polysilicon-based trap-rich layer. For foundries, wafer suppliers and SOI ecosystem partners, this creates a significant opportunity to advance RF and logic integration on SOI platforms.”

Traditional RF-SOI substrates rely on trap-rich layers to suppress parasitic surface conduction near the silicon/buried oxide interface. Without this suppression, RF signals can suffer from harmonic distortion, coupling loss and degraded passive-device performance. Acorn’s ABS technology introduces an ultra-thin buried silicon-germanium (SiGe) layer that can perform this trap-rich function in RF-SOI and FDSOI structures, while also introducing beneficial strain into the channel of FDSOI transistors.

“Acorn’s buried stressor technology is significant because it combines two important materials-engineering mechanisms in SOI structures,” said Professor Raskin of UCLouvain. “What is especially surprising and innovative is how effectively an ultra-thin silicon-germanium layer can function as a trap-rich layer, while also preserving the strain-engineering benefit for FDSOI. This combination has strong potential for future RF-FDSOI and RF-SOI technology development.”

Key characterization and modeling results include:

- **Carrier mobility:** Up to 50% estimated electron mobility improvement in FDSOI devices, with corresponding improvement in digital and RF figures of merit.
- **Prior FDSOI device results:** Measurements on advanced FDSOI devices with ABS showed improved transistor performance, including a 10% increase in saturation current and a 17% increase in transconductance.
- **RF nFET performance:** Simulated peak fT improved from 362 GHz to 442 GHz, while peak fmax improved from 385 GHz to 431 GHz.
- **RF substrate performance:** SiGe TRL behavior reduced harmonic distortion by suppressing parasitic surface conduction, with RF substrate metrics similar to commercial trap-rich RF-SOI substrates. An ultra-thin SiGe TRL also offers the potential for lower-cost implementation versus conventional thick polysilicon-based trap-rich layers.
- **Manufacturing compatibility:** Raman, TEM, PED and XRD analysis showed the integrated stress in the SiGe layer is largely preserved after high-temperature processing, including rapid thermal annealing at 1050°C.

Acorn is evaluating commercialization pathways for ABS with foundry, wafer and SOI ecosystem partners across RF-SOI and FDSOI platforms.

The post [Foundry-Compatible SiGe Trap-Rich Layer Technology Advances Next-Generation RF-SOI and FDSOI Platforms Share](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/foundry-compatible-sige-trap-rich-layer-technology-advances-next-generation-rf-soi-and-fdsoi-platforms-share/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Digest](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com).

items.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models
items.content:
*Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples.*

*Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview.*

**Q:**What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?

**A:** This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.

As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact.

I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better.

**Q:**Can you walk us through how the project has evolved?

**A:** When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved.

Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example.

Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques.

**Q:**What would you say are some recent highlights of your work?

**A:** Our [IPLoc research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.13317v2) was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context.

Then, we had an audio-based paper, [OmniR1](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=7Q1ApHpX31), that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are [multiple-choice answers](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/file/d6c01b025cad37d5c8bab4ba18846c02-Paper-Conference.pdf). A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks.

We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior.

**Q:**Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data?

**A:** These days, we can't create one of these very large foundation models ourselves. We don't have the resources to do that, so we're tending to use these available models and trying to adapt them, train them in a weakly supervised way, methods that don't require as much data, like our work on [test-time reinforcement learning](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026/papers/Singh_TTRV_Test-Time_Reinforcement_Learning_for_Vision_Language_Models_CVPR_2026_paper.pdf).

Our project was not monolithic, in the sense that we're not all working on one thing. It's more like a thousand flowers bloom, so there's no one particular way that we're approaching things.

**Q:**In the near future, how do you see multimodal research evolving in your MIT-IBM research team?

**A:** Over the years, we probably produced two dozen or so significant collaborative papers, and during this work, it was amazing to me that the machines could learn these correspondences without being told anything. No one had ever shown that machines could do it before we did that. Some of our early work combining audio with large language models was fun, too: seeing the model talk about what it heard and then having a conversation with it. Now, we are starting to take this for granted, but at the time, it was fun to see.

Moving forward, for the coming year, with our MIT-IBM collaboration, we're going to switch gears a little bit and focus more on what's known as full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. These are models that are listening while they’re talking, so it’s more like how humans operate, and this is quite different from what we’ve been doing up until now, which is joint audio-visual work, which we will also continue.

Now, we’ll be focusing on the speech side of things. These full-duplex models have suddenly become an interesting thing to look at, because they would move you away from the rigid turn-taking approach that is used right now when you're talking to some of these models. Ultimately, I think they will be more natural to interact with.

These full-duplex models are just starting to emerge, and some of the ones that are publicly available aren't as good as the big, large language models. They can handle some of these low-level communication skills, but they're still missing some things, like the concept of time, or knowledge depth. So, we're working on trying to address some of these issues.

*This research has been conducted in coordination with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab teams of* [*Rogerio Feris*](https://research.ibm.com/people/rogerio-feris)*,* [*Brian Kingsbury*](https://research.ibm.com/people/brian-kingsbury)*, and* [*Samuel Thomas*](https://research.ibm.com/people/samuel-thomas) *of IBM Research, and* [*Hilde Kuehne*](https://hildekuehne.github.io/about.html) *of the University of Tuebingen, who is an MIT-IBM affiliated researche*r.

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) or [Vercel](https://vercel.com/) that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

## Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/a-leaky-ai-supply-chain-is-exposing-secret-user-data-at-an-alarming-rate/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/a-leaky-ai-supply-chain-is-exposing-secret-user-data-at-an-alarming-rate/#comments)

items.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
items.content:
Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”

Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.

“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”

items.title: New approach enables physically consistent AI models of chaotic systems
items.content:
Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time.

Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology.

The new findings are [published](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2533077123) in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)* in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.

“Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.”

Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult.

“Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world.

“Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS.

“A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems.

“It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?”

“We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos.

Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says.

To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.”

He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.”

The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions.

Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.”

“AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.”

The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.”

“The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is [now accessible online at PNAS](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2533077123).

A [follow-up work](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v331/goertzen26a.html) this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award.

“Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”

items.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
items.content:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

items.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too
items.content:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL\_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”

Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

*This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.*

items.title: Micron Is Down 32% in a Month. Can MU Stock Get Back to $1,000? - 24/7 Wall St.
items.content:
# Micron Is Down 32% in a Month. Can MU Stock Get Back to $1,000?

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

The selloff in AI infrastructure stocks has hit memory makers hard, and **Micron Technology** (NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction) is squarely in its path. Micron stock is down 32% over the past month to $605.35 in Wednesday afternoon trading. That decline began at $896.07 on October 20 and includes a 12% drop from where it last closed.

A 52-week high of $1,254.61 shows that Micron shares traded above $1,000 within the past year. Even after the drop, the company’s large gain for the year remains intact, built on record results from the AI memory boom. What’s changed is the market’s confidence in how long that boom can last.

## UBS Puts a Price Tag on the AI Payoff Question

In a note on November 20, **UBS** (NYSE:UBS) questioned whether AI spending can earn its keep. The bank noted that recent selling followed persistent pressure on chipmakers and cloud companies as investors questioned the scale of AI infrastructure investment, adding that “risk-reward in equities had become more balanced.” By UBS’s estimate, cumulative U.S. tech investment in AI infrastructure could reach $5 trillion<sup>\[1\]</sup> by the end of 2028. UBS maintained that AI model and application revenues likely need to hit at least $1.5 trillion<sup>\[1\]</sup> by 2030 for an adequate return.

Another line in the UBS note lands close to home for Micron. The firm stated it’s “cautious on leveraged capacity providers, lower-quality suppliers, and companies whose valuations depend on persistent bottlenecks or distant cash flows.” Micron’s adjusted gross margin reached 87%<sup>\[2\]</sup> in Q4 FY2026. The firm said that level was built on tight memory supply and rising prices.

On its Q4 call, Micron’s management pushed into that tight-supply story. President and Chief Operating Officer Manish Bhatia offered the view. He said, “We made the statement that we really don’t have line of sight to when supply and demand balance.”<sup>\[3\]</sup> Industry trackers turned more conservative on memory pricing in recent days, putting that assumption under pressure.

Rates add pressure on Micron, with UBS expecting 25 basis point<sup>\[1\]</sup> Federal Reserve rate hikes in December and March 2027. That call followed Fed minutes showing nearly all policymakers expected further tightening, though UBS doesn’t anticipate a prolonged tightening cycle.

## Western Digital and Seagate Slide Alongside Micron

**Western Digital** (NASDAQ:WDC) stock is down 28% over the past month to $260.65. The hard disk drive (HDD) maker is also down 12% from its previous close, even after its Q1 FY2027 revenue grew 55.5%<sup>\[4\]</sup> year over year to $4.38 billion.

Meanwhile, **Seagate Technology** (NASDAQ:STX) stock is down 32% over the past month to $459.47. The decline includes a 12% drop from its previous close, even as Seagate’s guidance calls for Q2 FY2027 revenue of $4.8 billion<sup>\[5\]</sup>, plus or minus $100 million.

What separates Micron from both peers is the product. The company makes dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), NAND flash and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that works directly alongside AI processors. Following the spinoff of its flash business, Western Digital is a pure-play HDD company, while Seagate builds its drives around its heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) Mozaic platform.

## What Micron Needs to Reclaim $1,000

Micron’s road back to $1,000 likely requires firm memory pricing, strong guidance at the company’s next report, and evidence that AI spending is still growing. A high bar is already in place, since Micron’s latest guidance calls for Q1 FY2027 revenue of $61.5 billion<sup>\[2\]</sup>, plus or minus $1.5 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of $38.15, plus or minus $1. That outlook followed the company’s Q4 revenue of $54.23 billion<sup>\[2\]</sup>, up 379.3% year over year.

Most of Micron’s fiscal 2027<sup>\[3\]</sup> shipments are already committed, according to management, with customer allocation talks reaching into 2028. UBS struck a constructive note too. The bank wrote, “We do not think that the economic expansion, corporate earnings cycle, or structural AI investment story has broken.” Wall Street’s consensus price target of $1,561.91 serves as the bull-case marker for Micron.

## Micron’s $1,000 Question Comes Down to AI Returns

The bulls can point to committed shipments, long-term customer agreements and a supply picture that Micron’s management calls tight through 2028<sup>\[3\]</sup>. The next test for Micron is whether its next outlook confirms that pricing is holding up.

UBS’s warning about valuations built on persistent bottlenecks gives the bears their cleanest argument against Micron, especially if memory pricing moderates. Riding an AI mania is fine while it runs, but planning the exit matters just as much, something we covered in a free handbook here: The Bubble Survivor’s Handbook. Rate hikes could add pressure, and the steep slides at Western Digital and Seagate suggest a rebound may need the whole group to steady. So, a conservative investment approach may be wise until the AI spending return question resolves.

items.title: 新华社评论员：担当大国责任，共建美好世界
items.content:
新华社深圳11月20日电 **题：担当大国责任，共建美好世界**

新华社评论员

这是一次载入史册的“和平峰会”。19日下午，国家主席习近平在深圳同俄罗斯总统普京、美国总统特朗普举行中俄美元首会晤，就事关全球和平安全与稳定的重要问题深入交换意见，取得了一系列共识，发表了面向世界的《中俄美元首和平宣言》。三国元首历史上首次举行面对面会晤，开创了三国最高领导人交往的新纪录，为新时期大国互动构建了新范式，也是推进新型大国关系的新实践，是国际关系史上的重大创举。

大国和则世界安，大国斗则世界乱。和平是人类社会的永恒期盼。回望历史，80多年前，作为世界反法西斯的中坚力量，中俄美三国并肩奋战，取得伟大胜利，为世界赢得和平和安宁。放眼当下，世界百年变局加速演进，各种风险挑战层出不穷。作为世界主要大国和联合国安理会常任理事国，中俄美肩负着特殊责任，大国良性互动不是选择题，而是必答题。通过会晤加强沟通、管控分歧、稳定关系，符合三国共同利益，符合国际社会对和平与稳定的普遍期待，具有重要而深远的意义。

历史性的会晤，彰显为世界谋和平的大国担当。作为负责任大国，中国一贯主张大小国家一律平等，致力于实现国际关系的民主化，构建平等有序的多极化，认为大国拥有更多资源、更大能力，应展现大国胸怀、大国担当，在国际上带头讲平等、守诚信、尊道义、重合作、作表率。会晤期间，习近平主席高瞻远瞩，郑重提出坚持相互尊重、坚持和平共处、坚持合作共赢、坚持对话协商等4点看法，为走出一条大国正确相处之道进一步指明方向。

相互尊重是大国交往的基本准则。要彼此尊重、求同存异、共同发展，坚持不干涉别国内政，不干涉彼此内部事务，在涉及对方的重大敏感问题上提前沟通、换位思考、谨慎行事，特别是不能触碰对方的底线。“修昔底德陷阱”绝不是宿命。中俄美要做伙伴、做朋友，不冲突、不对抗，守住和平共处底线，坚定维护战后国际秩序，维护《联合国宪章》宗旨，捍卫来之不易的二战胜利成果，尽一切努力防止核战争。中俄美三国发展禀赋不同，经济互补性强。要加强经贸合作，实现双赢共赢，共同维护能源产业链供应链稳定畅通，维护全球能源市场安全稳定。大国间有分歧在所难免。要保持常态化高层交往，畅通各层级对话渠道，建立危机沟通和预防机制，确保误判少发生、分歧管得住、摩擦不升级。

作为一次具有开创意义的历史性会晤，中俄美元首会晤是积极的、建设性的，也是富有成果的，向世界释放了合作应对全球性挑战、促进世界和平稳定的鲜明信号。三国元首面对面阐明各自战略意图，愿意防止发生冲突对抗，守住和平共处底线，期待形成和平共处、总体稳定、均衡发展的大国关系格局。三国都记得二战期间并肩作战的历史，强调要珍惜来之不易的和平，大国应该重视各国合理安全关切；对话谈判是化解分歧的正确选择，只要对话不停止、大门不关上，和平就有希望；合作是应对挑战的必由之路，要基于共同利益加强合作，以合作促和平、谋共赢。会晤发布的《中俄美元首和平宣言》凝聚了三方共识，对更有效应对全球性挑战，维护好世界和平稳定具有重大积极意义。

习近平主席深刻指出，今天三国元首会晤播下的种子，必将生根发芽、开花结果。探索大国正确相处之道是一项长期任务，需要各方共同努力，呼唤久久为功的扎实行动。全面高效落实三国元首会晤共识，继续加强沟通，以对话聚共识，以担当迎挑战，以合作促和平，中俄美就能够为变乱交织的国际形势注入更多稳定性和正能量，共同推动建设一个更加美好的世界。

items.title: TSMC’s Supplier Awards Put Manufacturing Execution in Focus
items.content:
*“Amid macroeconomic uncertainties, TSMC’s confidence in continuous investment and growth stems from the deep trust we share with our supply chain partners,” said Dr. C.C. Wei, TSMC Chairman and CEO. “Our goal has always been to unleash our customers’ innovation and enable their success. Only through the close and agile collaboration of the grand alliance can we overcome challenges and transform technology breakthroughs into powerful momentum driving the industry forward.”*

Semiconductor break throughs are usually described in terms of smaller transistors, faster processors and more sophisticated packaging. But delivering those advances requires an extensive network of equipment manufacturers, materials specialists, construction contractors and production support companies. TSMC’s supplier awards offer a useful reminder that manufacturing leadership depends on how effectively that network performs.

At its confirmed 2025 Supply Chain Management Forum, TSMC recognized suppliers supporting advanced process development, packaging, capacity expansion and its international manufacturing footprint. The company also increased its emphasis on construction safety, sustainability and localization. Together, those priorities reveal how the definition of supplier excellence is broadening as semiconductor manufacturing becomes more demanding.

The importance begins with execution. A manufacturing roadmap has commercial value only when the required processes can operate reliably at production scale. Equipment must arrive, meet specifications and remain productive. Materials must perform consistently. Facilities must provide the operating conditions that sensitive manufacturing processes require. Weakness in any one area can undermine progress elsewhere.

Supplier recognition therefore highlights capabilities that rarely appear in chip performance announcements but directly influence delivery schedules, manufacturing costs and customer confidence. A more dependable installation, faster technical response or better controlled material can contribute to production performance even when it produces no headline improvement in transistor density.

Advanced packaging makes this interdependence particularly relevant. Combining multiple components into a finished device introduces additional manufacturing interfaces and coordination requirements. The practical implication is that expanding wafer production alone cannot guarantee a corresponding increase in completed products. Packaging equipment, materials, inspection and supporting operations must develop alongside the front-end process.

TSMC’s earlier 2024 awards explicitly recognized advanced packaging support, technology collaboration, automation and global production assistance. That breadth illustrates why the supplier ecosystem should be understood as part of the manufacturing platform itself. Its effectiveness depends on coordination across activities that individual companies may manage separately.

International expansion adds another challenge. Replicating manufacturing capability requires more than replicating buildings and installing similar tools. Suppliers need appropriate service coverage, trained personnel, logistics arrangements and an understanding of local operating requirements. Localization can improve responsiveness, but building a capable local network takes sustained investment and qualification.

For customers, the significance is practical: announced capacity and dependable output are different milestones. Suppliers help determine how quickly a new facility becomes a stable source of production. Their readiness affects whether geographic diversification delivers the resilience customers expect.

Construction safety deserves equal attention. TSMC’s 2025 announcement described contractor safety records as a selection criterion and introduced a standalone award for construction safety performance management. This signals that project success encompasses how capacity is built, alongside when it becomes available.

The broader implication is that safety belongs within operational planning. Poor construction practices can cause injuries, interrupt work and weaken confidence in project execution. Recognizing strong safety management creates an incentive for contractors to develop repeatable practices rather than relying solely on completion targets.

Sustainability also has operational consequences. Improving equipment efficiency and reducing resource consumption can help address the demands associated with expanding manufacturing. For suppliers, these requirements create opportunities to distinguish products through operating performance across their useful lives, alongside their immediate processing capabilities.

**Bottom line:** The forum provides a view of the capabilities TSMC considers important to manufacturing success. Technology development remains essential, but dependable support, safe construction, resource efficiency and regional readiness increasingly shape execution.

That is why the announcement matters beyond the winners. It shows that semiconductor competitiveness rests on coordinated industrial capability: the ability to develop technology, build capacity and operate it consistently. The suppliers enabling those outcomes help determine whether ambitious roadmaps become products customers can actually buy.
